newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe wants politicians to put their stamp on euro.
newsitem.headline: Juppe wants politicians to put their stamp on euro.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe on Tuesday repeated calls for a European economic government to balance the power of a common central bank once the single currency is launched and said the euro must be an instrument for growth.

Juppe, speaking five days ahead of a French parliamentary election, condemned the "unacceptable resignation" of those who believe Europe is chained to lacklustre growth and held up the euro as a way of breathing new life into the economy.
"We must affirm that Europe, like other great economic zones of the world, has a vocation for strong growth," Juppe told RTL French radio in an interview.
"One of the ways of doing this apart from national policy...is to make the euro an instrument for growth," he said.
He said this meant politicians setting broad guidelines for economic policy, and ensuring the euro had a "realistic" value against the dollar on its launch in 1999.
"We cannot leave it up to the European central bank to do everything. There should be an economic government for Europe, as we have been asking for months and have now begun to obtain," Juppe said.

The remarks reflected increasing attention to Europe in the last week of campaigning, though they were little different from those of Socialist leader Lionel Jospin who has insisted on the need for a European economic government.

European Union ministers have agreed to set up an informal stability council to co-ordinate economic policy inside the euro zone, though France's partners have insisted this will not be an "economic government" and will have no real power.
Juppe also said that France's place in a single currency could be endangered if a Socialist-Communist government shared power with conservative President Jacques Chirac.
"Cohabitation" -- the name the French give to power-sharing between a president and a government of different parties -- would be an obstacle to European integration and economic growth," he said.

"It would be a shambles in Europe, firstly because the Socialists and Communists don't agree among themselves...and also because the Socialists' economic policy, with extra spending and deficits, would push us out of the lane for European (monetary) union," he added.
Jospin's party has rejected calls by French communists, who may help form a government if the left wins the election, to pull out of the Maastricht plan for European monetary union.
But it says it will proceed only on four conditions, which include a new solidarity and growth pact to directly tackle unemployment, now running at a record 12.8 percent in France.
The party also wants to avoid the euro being overvalued against the dollar, which it sees as a threat to exports, and Italy and Spain included in the currency club from the start.

Juppe did not tackle the timing of those countries' membership directly, but said a key advantage of monetary union was that it would prevent "competitive devaluations" of the Italian lira which had harmed particularly French textile firms.

He said the stability pact agreed in Dublin last year had given politicians the power to decide the "broad choices of economic policy and especially the targets for growth, which should not be left solely to central bank governors".
Jospin wants the pact reviewed if the left wins control of the National Assembly in a two-round poll on May 25 and June 1.
Pollsters said on Saturday Juppe's centre-right coalition was poised to stay in power with a reduced majority. Fresh opinion polls cannot be published in the week to the election.
